coverage.narration: Floating neighborhoods are not science fiction. In Amsterdam, a floating neighborhood called Schoonschip is home to 46 households, a little over 100 people. Much larger designs exist on paper. One, for 12,000 people off the coast of Busan in South Korea, was unveiled in 2022, and when we checked in November 2026, its architects still listed it as in design.

coverage.narration: Look at two identical platforms carrying different buildings, one with two stories and one with four. Floating on their own, their decks would sit about 66 centimeters apart in height. So different loads add a demand on whatever connects them. In this design, the walkways between platforms are hinged, so they can follow the difference. Adding ballast to even out the decks would be another option.

coverage.narration: Connections are where engineers expect trouble. A 2026 research agenda lists stress concentrations on connectors among the challenges of large floating developments. One concept study links its modules flexibly, and spaces them far enough apart not to collide, because on flexible moorings they are expected to move sideways quite a lot.

coverage.narration: How many platforms would 10,000 people need? Say each resident needs about 40 square meters of floor: thirty for their home, and ten for a share of schools, shops and services. That's about thirty-three hectares of platform: about 200 platforms like our first one, with hundreds of connections between them.

coverage.narration: Bigger platforms mean fewer connections. At 100 meters on a side, 34 would do, but each would weigh about 30,000 tons, to build, launch and tow. Even the Schoonschip floats were too big for the dry docks of traditional houseboat builders, and were cast on the quay instead. Our district uses 60-meter platforms with three-story homes, 93 of them: a middle choice for this illustration, not an optimum.

coverage.narration: So the first fix is where you build. A 2026 concept study looks for sea areas with limited fetch, near a gulf, a strait or an archipelago, where waves stay moderate. That's why our city sits in a sheltered bay, connected to an existing city on shore.

coverage.narration: The second fix is the layout. Following one concept study, homes go in the middle, and functions that can tolerate more motion form the outer ring. Where the bay opens to the sea, a breakwater reduces the waves. But a floating breakwater may not be enough against longer waves from the open sea, and how much wave energy passes behind one is still hard to predict.

coverage.narration: Wastewater is separated there too: gray water from showers and washing machines, black water from toilets. Connecting floating homes to sewers on land takes extra infrastructure, such as waterproof cables and pumps. In our city, wastewater is pumped ashore along the bridges, and drinking water comes back the same way.
